paragraphs.text: Chapter 3. Stress Control

I, like everyone else, don't like the feeling of being stressed, but I have grown accustomed to the idea that life inevitably involves stress. Whether it was my high school classmates (most of whom were very driven), the athletes I've met, or the students, professors, and people in tech or creative fields around me, I have always found that stress accompanies ambition, and that for many of the top achievers, it's a constant. The weird thing is that many of the unambitious people I have known often said they were stressed out too. Lack of direction, lack of money, the feeling they were slipping behind in life, health issues, and more... Eventually I had to conclude that this was indeed part of life—like breathing, sleeping, or eating. That meant there had to be a good way to address it. The problem was that when I looked to see what the science said about stress, it was uniformly negative. It made Clear that stress wasn't just uncomfortable, it was damaging to the brain and body. And that only made stress more stressful. Moreover, the whole framing of stress seemed wrong, or at least rather one-sided. For instance, "fight or flight" is one of the most common phrases we hear when the topic of stress comes up. It's easy to remember and it seems science-y—because it sounds like it could describe how the brain and body respond to stress. Unfortunately, it's more misleading than informative. We also often hear that the stress response is an inconvenient holdover from our

evolutionary past. Meaning, the uncomfortable state of arousal we call stress was helpful for us long ago, propelling us to escape from sabertoothed tigers and other large predators, but it's no longer useful. I always appreciate when science shows up in a conversation, but I confess phrases like "fight or flight" make me shake my head. It's not just that they are misleading; they also don't provide any valuable information about how to navigate the stress response. And actually, the stress response is no holdover. And research has shown that the beliefs we hold about stress can change how stress impacts our health, for better or for worse, so we need to be careful what we tell ourselves about itu Stress is an area I've thought a lot about from a neuroscience perspective. My lab has studied it in animals and humans. Decades into my career, I now know that there is, in fact, a good way to address it. There are excellent stress management tools based in science. So, given how pervasive stress is, I am especially excited to share the information in this chapter. First let's begin with the facts. Forget sabertoothed tigers. Many of the same situations that stress us out now have been stressing out humans for thousands of years. An argument with a loved one, a persistent pain of unknown cause, a worry about a child, a looming payment, and on and on. Scenarios like these are not unique to modern times. A good way to think about stress is this: Stress is nature's attempt to create a single solution to all matters that might be, or actually are, urgent. 1'11 say that again. Stress is nature's attempt to create

extreme, it can make people feel as if they have left their body, as if they are viewing themselves from above. While that all sounds dreadful, we must remember that the stress response is adaptive. The purpose of it is to put our brain and body into a state that gives us the best chance of addressing the problem at hand. A single solution. In an ideal world, the degree of stress response would perfectly match the stressor we face. Running late? A little bit more arousal to help us focus on the key items we need to get out the door with grace would be perfect. See our toddler running toward the tramc? A huge surge in energy to quickly grab them is what we want! In fact, the parts of our nervous system that govern stress—called the autonomic nervous system—can be calibrated to generally match our stress level to the stressor we face, from mild to severe, from brief to ongoing.4 But nowadays, the many comforts most people enjoy thanks to technology—indoor heating and air conditioning, abundant food and shelter, and all in all our general lack of actual survival stressors—have our autonomic nervous systems uncalibrated. We are far more labile under the constant barrage of minor psychological stressors all day and night, and a lot of people are in a constant state of stress related to things they simply cannot control or influence even slightly. Put simply, the frequency and/or magnitude of the stress response is far too high relative to the stressors many people face. The occasional bout of stress lasting a few hours or less is no big deal, and even a few days is something our bodies can handle without long-term consequences. Once we experience a

few weeks to a month or more of daily (which usually also means nightly) stress, that's when we start to suffer. Chronically elevated resting blood pressure and heart rate, not sleeping well or enough due to rumination or feeling "tired but wired," and other shifts to our internal state become detrimental to our immediate and longterm health. We've all heard the laundry list of things that stress harms: our hormones, memory, mood, and decision-making ability, as well as the many diseases it makes worse or can bring about to our heart, brain, gut, and liver. The body of evidence that chronic stress is bad for us is vast and robust. Yet some stress is good for us. In fact, the occasional spike in our stress hormones can increase testosterone5 and improve our immune system functioning during the hours that follow. In the short term, it can improve our memory. The problems arise when the intensity or the duration of the stress response is too great. Eliminating stress from our lives is unrealistic. So our goal with stress should be twofold. First, we need to be able to adjust the intensity and the duration of our stress response so we can better handle stress in the moment. Second, many of us need to increase our stress threshold —that is, the subjective point at which events and thoughts trigger large arnounts of adrenaline release in our body—so our stress response is calibrated to any stressors we may encounter. Ahem, I mean, that we Will encounter. When adrenaline release occurs as the consequence of tiny things, that is not good. It negatively affects our physical health and relationships, including our relationship with ourselves. Do you like being

around you when you're stressed? Didn't think so. We can change our relationship to stress through cognitive reframing, but an effective approach is to learn to quickly control our stress response once it hits, and to periodically reset our stress threshold to a level that best serves us. We can't always control what life throws at us, but we can indeed control our stress response, and we can raise our stress threshold. That's what this chapter is all about. I first became interested in investigating the neuroscientific mechanisms behind stress back in 2015. At the time, grit, resilience, and mental toughness were popular themes in books and media. And those are great qualities. The examples—both historical and contemporary—of people being gritty and resilient and mentally tough are there to remind us that humans harbor within them an enormous capacity to manage and even channel their stress. While there is a lot known about the neural circuits and hormones that control the stress response, I specifically wanted to understand the mechanisms that determine its intensity and duration. I wanted to know which features of the stress response, like heart rate, blood pressure, attentional narrowing, and so on, were amenable to adjustment in real time. I also wanted to know whether there are levers for adjusting the duration, the intensity, and maybe even the probability of the stress response getting triggered in the first place. I was able to find some data about stress inoculation,$ including some studies supporting the idea that certain forms of early-life stress can set the stage for resilience later in life by

hot baths, deep breaths, talk therapy. Great! Who doesn't love a massage at the end of a hard day? Meditation is powerful as a tool to buffer against the stress response; a randomized clinical trial conducted by researchers at Georgetown University found that people with generalized anxiety disorder who meditated experienced a noteworthy reduction in pro-inflammatory cytokines—chemical messengers essential to our immune system but that can also trigger a stress response—compared to those who didn't meditate.&? Other studies, including one done by my lab at Stanford in collaboration with my colleague David Spiegel's lab, also at Stanford, have shown Clear benefits of meditation practices as short as five minutes per day on stress, mood, and sleep.J-3 That might seem like a trivial level of time commitment, especially given the many benefits of meditation. But I wanted to know how people can navigate stress while they are in the throes of the stress response. When their pulse is racing, their vision is blurry, their hands are shaking, and all they can think about is the stressor and the potential bad outcomes from it. That's when the capacity to manage stress matters most. Not offline, but in the moment. As I pointed out above, the stress response is universal. Whatever the specific stressor might be, the stress response is the same. It varies in degree, not kind. This suggests that if we have reliable tools to reduce the stress response in one context, we ought to be able to reduce it in another. The problem? No one had dissected the universal features of stress control, only the stress response.

One valuable thing everyone should know about the stress response, though, is that it is asymmetric: It starts extremely fast and turns off relatively slowly. The adrenaline release that is the first domino of the stress response happens in seconds or less and can continue for several minutes after we perceive a stressor.J5 Think of a time when you were groggy from just waking up and you picked up your Phone to see a disturbing text. BOOM! You are Wide awake and ready to move in an instant. That's the speed of adrenaline in action. Then, even after the stressor is resolved, the stress response persists. Imagine getting a text that says, "I think Mom was on the flight that just crashed," and ten minutes later, "I just spoke to her, she wasn't on there. She's fine." Your feeling of relief Will no doubt outpace how quickly your body settles down. That's an extreme example, but the same thing applies when someone almost sideswipes you while driving, and you swerve just in time to avoid a collision. A Shot of adrenaline wicks out through your body in an instant, and almost as fast, norepinephrine is released to ramp up attentional circuits in your brain. Cognitively, you realize you're safe almost as quickly as you thought you were about to get hit, but your body and mind don't relax immediately. More often than not, we plummet into the stress response and it takes time to return to baseline. And that's when everything turns out Okay. When stressors persist, you experience wave after wave of adrenaline. And while the basic circuits for stress are the same in everyone, seldom discussed is that not everyone has the same threshold, or trigger point, for a stress response to kick off For some

people it's as if that first domino is fixed in cement. Such people are rare. For most people, however, the domino falls too easily. I wanted to understand this aspect of stress too, in order to develop tools anyone can use to raise their stress threshold, to allow them to calibrate their autonomic set point. That is, the balance point that our nervous system works to maintain—so that the stress response happens when it's needed and not when it isn't. Even better would be to find ways such that when stress does happen, it occurs in proportion to the stressor. I wanted these tools to be mechanistic and behavioral, not pharmacological, because pharmacological tools —while they can be helpful—don't allow for realtime adjustments. You swallow a pill and that's that. And they have to be taken before stress arrives, which is problematic because we don't always know when stressors are coming. I also wanted to develop tools that do not rely on practice, like cognitive behavioral therapy, which is great but can take a fair amount of time to masterl and doesn't always translate across stressors very well; there is evidence both for and against generalizability.J-Z Like all protocols in this book, I wanted tools for stress management that could be effective the first time and every time because they are anchored in hardwired circuits and processes we all possess. So I dove into the research on the physiology of stress to come up with a different way to frame the whole concept of stress. And stress control. That led to. The Seesaw Model Think about the stress response as existing somewhere along a spectrum of arousal, with

in the daytime and asleep for a major portion of the night—then your SNS activity levels Will dominate in the daylight hours and your PNS Will dominate at night. In fact, the incredible impact your circadian rhythm has on your ability to reason,2 exert physical effort,2-W and resist infections22 stems from how it controls the balance of SNS versus PNS activity. In the morning and early daytime, elevated SNS activity (sometimes called "sympathetic tone") caused by a natural and healthy increase in our baseline levels of cortisol makes us physically stronger and better able to focus, whereas in the later evening and at night, when our baseline cortisol levels are markedly lower, our parasympathetic tone is elevated, and we become mentally and physically weaker, and our immune system becomes far less capable of warding off infections. (Circadian variation in the expression of specific genes and the actions of various molecules— neuromodulators, hormones, peptides, etc.—are what underlie those dramatic morning-versusnighttime variations in autonomic tone, as discussed in chapter 1 The second category of things that control our autonomic nervous system, and thus our level of arousal, are the sensory inputs—or stimuli, as neuroscientists call them—that we experience. For example, our level of physical comfort or pain, how well-fed or hungry we happen to be (not surprisingly, hunger makes us more alert), whether we are in a brightly lit or dim environment, the environment is quiet or loud, et cetera. And, of course, by the presence or absence of psychological stressors. In general, when we are hungry, thirsty, tired, or otherwise in need

of basic sustenance, our arousal levels increase and, with that, our propensity to think and move increases. It should be obvious Why that is adaptive. (It helps us seek out food, water, etc.) The third category of things that control our autonomic nervous system is pharmacologic. Caffeine and other stimulants are sympathomimetic, meaning they stimulate the SNS and increase arousal.24 Other drugs promote PNS activation, and thus decrease arousal levels. For example, alcohol and barbiturates indirectly increase PNS circuit activity,2 as does the molecule apigenin, which is found in chamomile tea" By the way, ifyou're wondering Why alcohol initially makes people more talkative and alert before it makes them drowsy or has them pass out, it's because before it reduces central nervous system activity and lowers arousal, alcohol first transiently stimulates the SNS. "It lifts you up before it drops you," as they say. Autonomic means "automatic" and indeed our sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems are, for the most part, not under our direct conscious control. We of course can adjust them indirectly. We just discussed three categories of ways to do that. The pathways and mechanisms by which different activities like exercise, or mechanical inputs like massage or a warm bath,2-g or drugs like caffeine22 elevate or lower arousal by adjusting the activity of our SNS or PNS are fairly well known, but again, it's crucial to note these are all indirect ways of adjusting autonomic arousal. As such, they tend to be Slow and hard to titrate—meaning hard to get just right. Moreover, some, like barbiturates or

prescription stimulants, have addictive potential and/or are costly. There is, however, one major exception to all of this: one lever by which we can quickly, directly, and reliably change our level of autonomic arousal by shifting the balance of SNS versus PNS activity. That lever is our respiration pattern, aka our breathing. Why? Because the neural circuits that control our breathing are part of our autonomic nervous system. In fact, they are the one (and only!) component of it that is both autonomic— breathing works just fine without us having to think about it—but that we can also consciously and directly control at any moment we choose. The same cannot be said about our heart rate, digestion, or immune system. As my colleague at Stanford, David Spiegel, MD, has described it to me, breathing and the neural centers that control breathing represent a bridge between our conscious and unconscious mind. We Will return to this idea shortly, but to understand the specific patterns of breathing that allow us to consciously and directly control our stress response, and to understand the best tools for adjusting our stress threshold, we need to take the autonomic spectrum—that continuum spanning from deep states of calm to intense states of panic I described earlier—and turn it into a seesaw. A seesaw? Correct. The simplest model for understanding how to control stress is a seesaw: parasympathetic at one end and sympathetic at the other. When the seesaw is tilted toward the parasympathetic end, we feel calm and relaxed. Tilt it further in that direction and we start drifting off to sleep. A flat, balanced seesaw

limits the range of solutions you can come up with to a problem.3-Z It even changes your ability to link previous experiences in insightful ways.33 Most of us are familiar with this stressinduced black-and-white thinking. These facts should help alleviate some of the frustration you may experience when someone tells you to "just relax," and you can't. Or when someone says, "Don't worry, this too Shall pass." The first form of encouragement ignores that we must actively do something to our physiology to relax. You can't out-think adrenaline. The latter encouragement is spot on, as stress does indeed hinder our ability to see the big picture, but it's not particularly helpful in the moment. It's sort oflike telling you that the splitting headache you're suffering from right now won't suck in the future. Fortunately, there is a way to get right to the physiology of the stress response. Rather than try to directly reduce sympathetic tone, you need to instead tilt the seesaw back toward the parasympathetic side by increasing the activity of your PNS. That is going to be the fastest way to calm down in real time whenever you are feeling stressed. Resilience defined If you think about it, this is a big part of what resilience is really about. It's not our ability to tolerate or eliminate the stress response but rather our ability to reduce its intensity quickly and in real time, when our arousal exceeds a useful level, so that we can move forward. Resilience is our ability to control stress. Sometimes that means going from extreme stress to very alert and energized, so we can perform a task and quickly problem-solve under intense

pressure. Other times it means taking ourselves from endlessly looping thoughts to deep sleep. Resilience is also about an ability to deliberately increase our stress threshold, so life's minor stressors don't disproportionally hijack our mind and body. Once you learn how to do those two things, then you Will truly be in the driver's seat. Maybe that all sounds overly simplistic. Easy to say but harder to do. Well, it turns out there are science-supported tools to adjust your stress response in real time and to raise your stress threshold, and they work exceedingly well—and fast. They can also work the first time, and every time, because they are grounded in biological mechanisms and circuits that you already have inside you and can access. Some involve adopting a specific pattern of breathing, but they are not breathwork. After all, when we find ourselves in a high stress situation, we can't run off and do five minutes of box breathing! Other protocols don't involve breathing at all. I've been blessed to play a partial role in the discovery and application of several of these stress control protocols, although like so many other scientific "discoveries," aspects of them were known about and used by nonscientists in other contexts first. None of us gets the patent. The following pages explain what they are, how they work, and how to use them.
STRESS CONTROL PROTOCOL Do One to Three Physiological Sighs to Reduce Stress Fast
WHAT TO DO

• Breathe in the pattern known as the physiological sigh. Inhale deeply through your nose until your lungs are full (your belly should expand out while you inhale), then sharply inhale a second time, also through your nose, to maximally inflate your lungs. Then slowly exhale through your mouth until your lungs are empty of air. Repeat this in-in-out breathing pattern up to three times, in succession, as needed to reduce your stress level (meaning, your level of autonomic arousal) fast.
HOW IT WORKS

Physiological sighs are, to my knowledge, the fastest and most effective way there is to deliberately calm yourself down. Often just one physiological sigh does the trick. That's because our state of mind and body changes our breathing but our breathing also changes our state of mind and body.3.4 Remember the locus coeruleus that releases norepinephrine to make us alert? Well, specific populations of

exhale. We need both oxygen and carbon dioxide, but we need them in the right balance. If we breathe too little, carbon dioxide builds up in our brain and bloodstream, leading to headaches and tiredness.3-$ If we breathe too much—rapidly inhaling and exhaling, or what we typically call hyperventilation—we expel too much carbon dioxide, which is problematic because carbon dioxide is crucial for making sure oxygen gets to our brain cells. If you've ever wondered Why it's advised to breathe into a paper bag if you're having a panic attack, it's to recapture some of the carbon dioxide that would otherwise be expelled. In this chapter you'll learn faster and better ways to calm down, but the logic is the same. Overbreathing causes anxiety, dizziness, confusion, poor sleep, and even muscle spasms. As mentioned in the introduction to this chapter, the neurons in our brainstem that control our breathing represent a bridge between our conscious and unconscious mind. They are equipped to sense the ratio of oxygen to carbon dioxide in our blood, which prompts any necessary alterations in our breathing pattern to keep us alive and well. That happens regardless of whether we are exercising hard or deeply relaxed —it even happens while we sleep.40 Unlike other autonomic neural circuitry, however, we can take immediate conscious control of these neurons. We can decide "I'm going to extend my next exhale a bit" or "I'm going to take one more inhale before holding my breath" and—voila!—we can make that happen. We just don't have that level of conscious control over any other autonomic function. There are some reported examples of people who used biofeedback to learn to directly

control their heart rate or the size of the pupils of their eyes, but that requires a fair amount of training.4J Extended exhales and physiological sighs are something that anyone can do. Certain internal states are associated with certain respiratory patterns. And by deliberately changing how we breathe, we can shift our internal state. That's a big deal and something I wish they had taught us in grade school. Alas, it wasn't until recently that Western science embraced controlled studies of respiration and, in doing so, revealed what had been known in Eastern traditions for thousands of years. We owe it to a small set of dedicated researchers, mostly neuroscientist Jack Feldman's lab at UCLA, for discovering how the brain controls breathing, both our unconscious reflexive breathing and deliberate breathing, and how they impact our emotional and cognitive states.4-Z Before and during our discussion on the Huberman Lab podcast, Jack told me stories of setting out to study this topic in the early 2000s, and a luminary of neuroscience making fun of him at meetings. He would jab: "Why would you study something as boring as breathing? Why don't you study something important, like (That guy studied memory.) Jack knew to ignore him and follow his intuition. His work ignited a field that is now positively impacting the mental and physical health of people of all ages. Detecting and modifying certain breathing patterns also turns out to be important for predicting heart attacks,44 strokes,45 and seizures,46 and for preventing sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS).4Z Some of his recent work has also shed light on the fact that some opioid drugs can lead

to death because of how they change the firing patterns of the neurons that control breathing. It is fair to say that Jack's work has literally saved lives. Breathing isn't just about getting oxygen into your lungs; it also helps control heart rate. While you can't directly control your heart rate, you can leverage the fact above and use your breathing to control it indirectly. Deliberately inhaling more vigorously or longer (or both) increases your heart rate, whereas deliberately exhaling more vigorously or for longer slows your heart rate down, through a process called respiratory sinus arrhythmia. Exhales also activate a specific branch of the vagus nerve, which is part of the PNS, which in turn reduces the rate of electrical activity in neurons of the sinoatrial node of the heart, your heart's natural pacemaker. So deliberately emphasizing the intensity and/ or duration of your exhales for a few breathing cycles Will caaaaalm youuuu dooooown. The breathing pattern described in this protocol does just that. Once you learn the relationship between breathing and heart rate, and deploy the physiological sigh to reduce your heart rate on the spot, it gives you a significant feeling of confidence in dealing with stress, and uncertain circumstances too. You no longer have to be afraid you Will get stuck in an anxiety response in a key moment, or any moment for that matter. You also realize that what most people say to themselves or others when stress hits—"Take a deep breath"—is the exact opposite of what we need to do! When stress hits we should do a big exhale. It is when

Thus, physiological sighs, unlike just a big exhale or box breathing, are a three-pronged tool to quickly (1) Slow your heart rate, (2) reestablish proper oxygen—to—carbon—dioxide ratios in your brain and bloodstream, and (3) engage brain areas that let you think logically about your situation. It's adaptive biological engineering at its best and works to calm you down. Infants do physiological sighs reflexively. Animals do too.5J Observe a dog right before it goes down for a nap. You'll see that double inhale, long exhale pattern. Rats physiological sigh when 5.2 placed into a claustrophobic environment. People reflexively do physiological sighs about once every few minutes when working5.3 and even in their sleep to reset their oxygen—to— carbon-dioxide ratio. In fact, you have dedicated sets of neurons in your brainstem for generating physiological sighs.55 Nature just doesn't create discrete neural pathways by accident; that's how important this breathing pattern is. One respiratory region, the pre-Bôtzinger complex, controls your rhythmic breathing, the regular alternation of inhales and exhales.5é But a second region, the parafacial nucleus, controls breathing that involves double inhales, double exhales, or any combination of inhales and exhales in ratios other than the 1:1 inhale-exhale pattern.5Z The parafacial nucleus does things other than generate physiological sighs but that's one of its primary functions. I'd like to clarify that physiological sighs are not breathwork. Breathwork refers to setting aside five to twenty minutes to do a specific breathing pattern (or designated sequence of patterns) to get you into a specific state of mind and body.

Physiological sighs are a naturally occurring breathing cycle that we can deliberately recreate. And they are the fastest way to consciously tilt your seesaw to the parasympathetic side of your autonomic nervous system. Do it before public speaking or a hard conversation. Do it when you're stuck in trafic or late to an important meeting and starting to feel your tension level rise. Do it to stop yourself from overreacting to an offhand comment. It won't guarantee that you'll always do the right thing in response, but it Will put you in a better frame of body and mind, so that you have the best chance of navigating the stress that comes from these or similar situations. There are data showing that doing physiological sighs outside of stressful moments 5.8 can help buffer you against future stress too. Several years ago, my lab collaborated with psychiatrist David Spiegel to investigate just that.5.2 We conducted a study that randomized 108 participants to one of four groups. One group did five minutes per day of cyclic physiological sighing: Inhale, inhale, long exhale, repeat, and so on for five minutes. The second group did five minutes per day of box breathing, a breathing technique I've mentioned before, which follows a pattern of inhale-hold-exhale-hold-repeat, where each inhalation and exhalation, and the holds, are the same duration, until five minutes have elapsed. The third group did five minutes per day of cyclic hyperventilation: You take a big deep breath in through the nose and a shorter exhale through the mouth, putting more vigor into the inhalation than the exhalation. A fourth group did five minutes per day of meditation, seated

with eyes closed, and focusing their attention on their breath but with no specific instructions about breathing pattern. Most participants, regardless of their group, reported an improvement in mood and outlook. But cyclic physiological sighing had a notably bigger effect. We also observed improvements in resting heart rate, improved sleep, and other metrics of well-being related to autonomic function. In other words, doing one to three physiological sighs is a great tool for when stress hits and doing five minutes of physiological sighs on repeat can help buffer us further against the inevitable stress of life. Given what you now know about exhales slowing heart rate, oxygen and carbon dioxide levels, and the autonomic seesaw, it should make sense as to Why this works. Your brain and body were literally built to do this.
STRESS CONTROL PROTOCOL Use Deliberate Cold Exposure to Raise Your Stress Threshold
WHAT TO DO

• Put yourself in uncomfortably cold water three to seven times per week. This can be as simple as a cold shower, or as involved as an ice bath. For the duration, choose one ofthese options: • Timed protocol: One to three minutes per session. • Count "walls of adrenaline" protocol: Rather than committing to a specific amount of time, try committing to a specific number of mental "walls" to climb over. When you feel the impulse to avoid or exit the cold but you stay, that's one wall you've scaled. Decide in advance how many times you Will encounter this impulse and keep going. You do not have to always increase the number of walls. There are days when you Will decide to "go over" five walls and other days where two walls Will be enough. • The water should be uncomfortably cold. This means it should immediately trigger your

the strength and hypertrophy adaptations that would otherwise occur. (Chapter 2 explains more about those adaptations, and how to achieve them.) That inhibition of muscle growth is likely due to the vasoconstriction the cold causes, which limits both nutrient delivery and waste removal from the recently trained muscles and also blunts protein synthesis.60 Wait at least Six hours after resistance training to do deliberate cold exposure, or do it before you train, or just save it for another day. Or do it any time relative to your resistance training, but be sure to end with a hot shower or bath to reestablish perfusion of the muscles to correct for this. One study argued that deliberate cold exposure done in the first Six hours after resistance training does not prevent strength adaptations, but most of the work on this issue indicates that deliberate cold exposure done in the Six hours or so after resistance training Will significantly reduce any hypertrophy or strength increases that would otherwise occur. 1 So it is best to simply do it before resistance training, or on rest days. Or allow Six or more hours to elapse after resistance training before deliberate cold exposure. Another common myth is that deliberate cold exposure is harmful for people wishing to limit their cortisol levels. You often hear that people should avoid deliberate cold exposure to keep their cortisol levels low too. Yet the cortisol increases caused by deliberate cold exposure, while significant, are transient and small compared to the dramatic increase that a moderate intensity exercise session triggers. You won't hear that people should avoid exercise to keep cortisol low because the cortisol increase

caused by exercise is, again, transient and, what's more, beneficial. (Indeed, it is a key aspect of the specific and general adaptation triggers we discussed in chapter 2). Many of the "cold exposure is bad for you" stories involve people going into the cold for very long periods of time at excruciatingly cold temperatures, or combining deliberate cold exposure with hyperventilation breathwork and/ or jumping or diving under ice. All of which are dangerous and should be avoided. Now that those points are out of the way, let's look at Why deliberate cold exposure is beneficial. Done correctly, deliberate cold exposure is a powerful, safe, and reliable tool for rapidly adjusting your internal state and stress threshold. There are two key phases, each with distinct benefits. First, the state shift that occurs during the cold exposure itself. Second, the state shift that occurs for many hours afterward. Anyone who has done deliberate cold exposure consistently—that is, three to seven times per week—will tell you there is a third phase too, which is the change in your subjective experience of stress and your ability to navigate other forms of stress. When you enter the cold, it sharply tilts your autonomic nervous system toward the sympathetic end of the seesaw. It does this the first time and every time, and it happens fast, within one to two seconds upon entering the cold. Then, once you get out of the cold, you tend to remain in a very "alert but calm" state—meaning (in the context of the model I described) with an evenly balanced autonomic seesaw—for many hours afterward.

Deliberate cold exposure increases the levels of circulating catecholamines in your brain and body: adrenaline, norepinephrine, and dopamine, and increases in the hormone cortisol too. Some, including dopamine in particular, remain elevated long after you dry off and warm up. These catecholamines increase mood, energy, and alertness. They also can increase your stress threshold; more on that below.65 But first I want to pause for a moment because you may be asking this: Why would I want to trigger the release of these "stress" chemicals? Won't that make me feel more, not less, stressed? Yes, but that's what this protocol is all about. We need to challenge the notion that stress is always bad for us. In fact, when we have control over when, how much, and especially for what purpose we experience stress, the impact of that stress can switch from being health-perturbing to healthpromoting, and this reshapes the body's response to all forms of stress.6é This is not "mind over matter," it's leveraging the brain circuits that convert the arousal response we call stress into something called eustress a term coined by Swiss physiologist Hans Selye.6Z (You may remember him from the previous chapter.) He was nominated for the Nobel Prize seventeen times for his work on this and related topics, long before we knew what the underlying mechanisms were, but as those mechanisms have become elucidated, many of his theories have largely been deemed correct. We now know that your prefrontal cortex —that patch of brain real estate involved in context-dependent decision-making (as well as

Cortisol and the catecholamines adrenaline and norepinephrine, but especially cortisol, are often thought of purely as stress chemicals. The third catecholamine—dopamine—escaped this reputation but is usually thought of (also incorrectly) as purely a pleasure chemical. And while cortisol is involved in the stress response, thinking about it as purely a stress chemical is wrong. I wish I could banner this across the sky: Cortisol Is Not a Stress Hormone! In fact, if I could impart just one message about how to improve your health, it would be this: Strive to get your morning cortisol high (yes, high!) and your nighttime cortisol low.

The main function of cortisol is to ensure there is enough energy in the form of glucose, or blood sugar, for you to meet life's demands. Yes, that can include overcoming stressors, but it also includes simply waking up each morning with the physical and mental energy required for work, school, family, and exercise. Cortisol causes glucose (as well as fats) to get released into the bloodstream, and it also stimulates the liver to make more glucoseun Cortisol and adrenaline play additional key roles in our body's everyday functioning. They improve our immune system's ability to ward off infections, they elevate our mood, they allow for our capacity to form new memories, and they increase metabolism... so just forget the idea that cortisol and adrenaline are only about stress. A gradual rise in your cortisol levels starts three to four hours before you wake up each morning and its levels eventually hit a threshold level, at which point you wake up, open your eyes, and get out of bed. Keep in mind that cortisol doesn't act alone to rouse you from sleep; a parallel rise in body temperature and clearance of the sleepiness-inducing molecule adenosine follows a similar schedule. Nonetheless, scientists call this rise the "cortisol awakening response" or CAR. Now that makes it sound like a medical problem of some sort, but CAR is a normal and (provided it is timed correctly) health-promoting aspect of our biologyu-Z And it helps buffer you against unhealthy stress. Cortisol first starts to rise as a result of a signal from your SCN, your brain's master circadian clock that we discussed in chapter 1. For most people, that rise starts somewhere around

five hours into their night's sleep and continues sharply over the subsequent two to three hours until it reaches a threshold level and bam! You wake up. Even if you use an alarm clock, you can be sure your cortisol levels were rising as you approached the start of your day. Now, once you're awake, cortisol continues to increase until it hits its peak for that twenty-four-hour cycle. For most people, that peak occurs anywhere from 0.5 to 1.5 hours after waking up. Then cortisol levels slowly start to decline— a process that continues into the late afternoon and evening. Assuming you encounter no major stressors, your cortisol levels continue to drop in the hours before you fall asleep and reach their lowest level about three to four hours after you doze off, and then slowly start to rise again to eventually trigger the next morning's CAR, and so on. This is the ideal cortisol pattern for mental and physical health, energy, and resilience to stress. Ashwagandha: Ashwagandha, also known as Indian ginseng or winter cherry, is used as an adaptogen— a term that broadly refers to substances that improve a person's resistance to stress. A large review published in 2021 that included fortyone total studies in humans included seven that focused on stress and anxiety, enrolling a total of 491 adults who either reported being under high stress or were diagnosed with an anxiety disorder. I Ashwagandha dosages varied from 240 milligrams per day to 1,250 milligrams per day for an extract and up to 6,000 milligrams when administered as a powdered root. (Most ashwagandha capsules sold over the counter in the US contain 200—600 mg per capsule.) Taken together, these studies showed that ashwagandha reduced stress and anxiety when compared to a placebo, and also reduced sleeplessness and fatigue. Cortisol levels in the blood were also lower among people taking this supplement, and it appeared that the cortisol-lowering effect of ashwagandha is likely the major basis of its effect on lowering stress and anxiety. A study of Sixty adults found that those who took 225 milligrams or 400 milligrams per day of ashwagandha reported reductions in anxiety, depression, and food cravings compared to people randomized to a placebom One study found that men and women taking ashwagandha had a 22 percent and 25 percent reduction in cortisol, respectively,

Most likely the effect is due to a "cocktail" of several different compounds in ashwagandha that work in parallel on various aspects of the hypothalamic-pituitaryadrenal axis, which, as you may remember from Sleep Protocol 1, is our main biological circuitry for mobilizing a physiological response to a stressor. The most potent of these mechanisms is the suppression of the signaling pathway for corticotropin (ACTH), a hormone that acts to stimulate the release of cortisol from your adrenals.J3.3 The ashwagandha-suppression of corticotropin (ACTH) happens through a multistep process that begins with compounds called withanolides (naturally occurring plant hormones). These compounds can lower corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) in the hypothalamus.J-34 Limiting the amount of CRH in turn dampens the signaling that would normally trigger the release of cortisol. The fact that ashwagandha works "upstream" from the adrenal glands has a potential downside: Namely, it is likely to impact all the biology connected to CRH, which includes the gut and the immune system, among others. That's one of several reasons Why I suggest not taking ashwagandha at dosages higher than 600 milligrams per day for more than a few weeks before taking at least a few weeks off. There is at least one report of someone taking a high dose (950 mg) of ashwagandha daily for a year and developing adrenal insuficiency. People seem to vary quite a bit in their sensitivity

Phosphatidylserine: Phosphatidylserine is a type of phospholipid. It is naturally found in the membranes of neurons, and comprises about 10 to 20 percent of the total phospholipid content of the brain—an enormous percentage when one considers that much of the nonliquid content of the brain is phospholipids. Naturally occurring phosphatidylserine plays a role in cognitive function,J-43 and the loss of phosphatidylserine in neurons known to occur in later adulthood may partially explain age-related (non-dementia) cognitive decline. What's more, in its natural state in our brains, this compound is known to decrease the stress response.U44 As a supplement, phosphatidylserine has shown some benefit in Older adults who experience chronic stress. There is some evidence phosphatidylserine taken late in the day may preferentially reduce evening and nighttime cortisol,U4.5 which may explain how it indirectly supports sleep. In one investigation, from 2004, participants took a phosphatidylserine supplement at a dose of 400 milligrams, 600 milligrams, or 800 milligrams, or a placebo (twenty people per group) and then completed a type of social stress test that involves performing in front of an audience.J-46 Data collected on biological indicators of the stress response revealed a significant decrease in these symptoms among

Another study found no link between phosphatidylserine and measures of a stress response across all Sixty participants, but the researchers did observe an effect among participants with high chronic stress levelsl Initially, this group had a diminished cortisol rise in response to a social stress test.
